Pause for two seconds at each question activity.

teacherGuide.overview: A story about how scientific ideas change. The oldest known Homo sapiens fossils are in Morocco; Ghana’s cave shows how people lived much later. The timeline walk gives learners a feel for deep time, and the DNA figure supports a conversation about human unity and variation.
learningGoals: Explain that our species is about 300,000 years old and that its origin involved many parts of Africa.
Build and read a scaled timeline.
Explain that people are genetically very similar and that science keeps changing.
beforeReading: Ask: where do you think the story of our species began?
whileReading: At page 5, ask learners to calculate steps before reading on.
afterReading: Build the timeline on the field and add events: school founded, Ghana’s independence (1957), Bosumpra’s first use, Homo sapiens.
discussion: What does it mean that the face looked modern but the braincase did not?
Why is “dispersal within Africa” an important idea?
reflection: What would you like scientists to find next?

mathsExtension.task: On a timeline of 1 step per 10,000 years, how many steps for 300,000 years?
How many years older is Jebel Irhoud (about 300,000) than Herto (about 160,000)?
About 3 billion DNA letters are in a human genome. 0.4% of 3 billion is how many letters?

support: Provide a printed timeline and fill in the dates.
stretch: Explain in one paragraph why a single oldest fossil does not prove where a species began.

culturalNotes: The story presents Ghana as part of the long human story: Bosumpra Cave on the Kwahu Plateau shows human use of a Ghanaian site for more than 10,000 years.
The story treats all people as one species and avoids ranking people or groups.
localiseThis: Add local archaeological sites if available; discuss with care that these are heritage places.
Keep discussion of human variation respectful; be ready to challenge any stereotypes that arise.

whatWeKnow: Fossils from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco, are about 300,000 years old and are the oldest securely dated Homo sapiens fossils.
Early Homo sapiens fossils are known from several parts of Africa, including Florisbad (about 260,000 years), Omo Kibish (about 195,000 years) and Herto (about 160,000 years).
On average, any two people’s genomes are about 99.6% identical.
Bosumpra Cave on the Kwahu Plateau was used for more than 10,000 years.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Exactly where and how our species first emerged, and how groups across Africa interacted.
How early people’s brains, thinking and language developed.
Whether older fossils remain to be found.

investigation.title: Walk through deep time
materials: A long rope or a measured path (at least 30 m)
steps: Choose a scale of 1 step (about 1 m) for 10,000 years.
Mark today as the start of the rope.
Place a marker at 1 step for Bosumpra’s 10,000 years and at 30 steps for Homo sapiens.
Add events your class chooses and discuss what the distances tell you.
investigation.whatToNotice: Human history takes up a very small part of the long history of the Earth.
investigation.safetyNote: Do the walk on a safe, flat area away from roads, in shade where possible.

factCheck.claim: Jebel Irhoud fossils are about 300,000 years old, the oldest securely dated Homo sapiens evidence; the face looks almost modern but the braincase is elongated and archaic; other early sites include Florisbad (about 260,000 years), Omo Kibish (about 195,000 years) and Herto (about 160,000 years).
factCheck.explanation: From the Max Planck Society summary of the 2017 research.
factCheck.reference: Max Planck Society, “The first of our kind” (mpg.de). Check for newer discoveries.

factCheck.claim: On average any two people’s genomes are about 99.6% identical (the older figure of 99.9% counts only single-letter differences).
factCheck.explanation: From the US National Human Genome Research Institute.
factCheck.reference: NHGRI, Human Genomic Variation fact sheet.

factCheck.claim: Bosumpra Cave (Abetifi, Kwahu Plateau) was used over more than 10,000 years; plant remains include Canarium and oil palm, and later domesticated pearl millet and cowpea.
factCheck.explanation: From a published study of the cave’s plant remains.
factCheck.reference: Vegetation History and Archaeobotany, 2015 (Springer); confirm details with an archaeologist.

reviewerNotes: Confirm first-syllable stress and final vowel.
